title: Why the Army Blew Up Five Tons of Its Own Explosives
fb_caption: On Wednesday at 9 a.m., in southeast Iowa, the US Army blew up about five tons of its own explosives, on purpose. The material was lead azide, a primary explosive normally used in tiny amounts inside detonators, and the Army said it had begun to crystallize in its drums. Crystals can make it even more sensitive, so explosives like this could go off just from being moved. That is why disposal teams usually destroy them where they sit, behind barriers, foam and water. The EPA said its air monitors showed no lead in the air afterward; soil and surface tests were still to come. Would you watch a controlled blast from a safe distance, or stay far away? Tell us below.

The Army said the material had crystallized in its drums (found at a routine inspection in March), making it more sensitive and unsafe to move [Verified, 3 sources]: PBS; NBC; CBS (above)
Barriers, foam and large water tanks were set up around the bunkers; officials said the blast was driven into the ground [Verified, 2+ sources]: CBS; NBC; PBS

tts.director_notes:
Male documentary-style news explainer for a US/UK social video. Firm, authoritative and confident, punchy and fast (about 170-185 words per minute), conversational but serious. Short sentences, a brief dramatic pause before key facts, lively intonation, never monotone or salesy.
Pronunciation: azide = AY-zide (lead AY-zide); say "nine A M" and "nine fifteen" clearly.

beats.text: Wednesday. Nine A M. Southeast Iowa. The US Army blew up about five tons of its own explosives. On purpose.
Why would an army destroy its own stockpile? Follow the clock.
March. A routine inspection. The material is lead azide, and the Army said it had begun to crystallize inside its drums.

Lead azide is a primary explosive. Usually, a tiny pinch sits inside a detonator, and its job is to set off a much bigger charge. So it is built to be sensitive. Crystals can make it more sensitive still: to friction, to shock, even to cold. That creates a trap.
Explosives this touchy could go off just from being moved. So disposal teams usually stop trying to carry them away. They destroy them where they sit, at a moment they choose.
The days before. Crews raise barriers around the bunkers, and bring in foam and giant tanks of water, meant to soak up the blast and its dust.
Nine A M. Detonation. Officials said the blast was driven down, into the ground.
Nine fifteen. The Environmental Protection Agency said its air monitors showed no lead in the air. More than an hour later, it said the same. Soil and surface tests were still to come.

items: EPA: NO LEAD IN THE AIR
SOIL + SURFACE TESTS: STILL TO COME

beats.text: Takeaway: if you ever find an old shell, old ammunition, or damaged fireworks, don't touch it and don't move it. Back away, and call the authorities.

Would you watch a controlled blast from a safe distance, or stay far away? Tell us in the comments, and send this to someone who loves knowing how things work. Because on Wednesday at nine A M, the Army decided the safest way to move five tons of explosives was not to move them at all.
